doc.title: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack") Interview, 1959-07-01
doc.interviewee: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack")

title: The Monogram Theater and the origin of the presentation show
summary: They played the Monogram on 35th Street through the 1918 flu, sometimes two years at a stretch. Billy says Paul Ash saw their stage-show style and took it downtown, getting credit for the presentation show.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Do you remember? 1918. 1918. That's when the flu was. Oh, yes. I remember. I had the... Yes. Do you remember?

Oh, that's when almost the stage was signed, we were here. Yeah, we were here all through that time, but we stayed there quite a while. Yes. And we used to stay as long as two years, you know, at this one theater. That was on 31st Street? Yes, 35th. 35th. Monogram is 35th. The monogram?
The new monogram. Uh-huh. The old monogram was up to 35th, but they didn't have any
border to that. I never got to see that. I knew some of the theaters, like the Grand,

and they tore that down just a few weeks ago, I hear. And we had the style of presenting the show, was what they later called a presentation, but at the time, I didn't name it that, but there was a man downtown at the Oriental Theater called Paul Ash. Oh, yes. And he come out to the monogram and saw the style of show I was doing, and he took it downtown, and he got credit for
